statement: In healthy, screened adults given MDMA by mouth by researchers in laboratories, and a placebo on another day, MDMA raised ratings of the drug's effect, of a good effect and of feeling happy, and, in one study, of feeling open and close to others, and also raised ratings of a bad effect and of physical complaints, in the same sessions (five papers from Basel, Chicago, San Francisco and Zurich, not fully independent: the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers a senior author, and one author is on four of the five). In 166 volunteers aged 18 to 45 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel, four in five new to MDMA, the average highest self-rating of 'any drug effect' on a 0 to 100 line was 73 in men and 85 in women after 125 mg (136 people), against 4 on placebo, and lower after 75 mg (30 other people); of 'good drug effect' it was 77 and 82 after 125 mg, against 3 or 4. Four of the 166 reported no effect. The effect began on average 33 minutes after the dose (SD 24), peaked at 1.6 hours (SD 0.8) and lasted 4.2 hours (SD 1.3; range 1.4 to 8.2); in 16 volunteers in Zurich it began 20 to 120 minutes after the dose and lasted about 3 hours. In a 32-person Basel study (probably within the 166), ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others rose (F(1,31) 121, 81 and 68; p < 0.001), as did scores for well-being, extroversion and activity, with no rise in anxiety; in Zurich, positive mood averaged 40% of the highest possible score against 0.6% on placebo and thought disorder 25% against 0, with no rise in aggression-anger, apprehension-anxiety or depressiveness. The social effects are less settled: a 'sociable' rating rose at 1.5 mg/kg in 9 people in Chicago (+19.7 points against -6.3; p = .04, which the authors call marginal) while a friendliness scale did not change significantly; closeness was rated higher in San Francisco than in Basel; peak ratings of drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ significantly between three sites (220 volunteers, partly overlapping the others; no means printed, and no significant difference is not proof of equality); and empathy and money-sharing tests rose in one Basel study, in men only on post hoc tests. The same sessions brought unwanted effects. 'Bad drug effect' averaged 13 in men and 24 in women after 125 mg against 2 on placebo, higher in women also after allowing for dose per kilogram and blood level (SDs of 22 and 24, so ratings varied widely). In the first 6 hours, MDMA against placebo in 166 people: lack of appetite 59%, dry mouth 55%, difficulty concentrating 46%, cold feet 42%, sweating 41% and jaw clenching 40% (of 134 asked), against 0 to 6%; at 24 hours, lack of appetite 31% (1% on placebo), lack of energy 30% (3%) and headache 33% (15%). Nine people reported anxiety, all after 125 mg; the authors say verbal support reduced it and no benzodiazepine was used. The paper reports no serious adverse event, depressed mood in 4% after 125 mg in the next one to two weeks, and 'flashbacks' (not defined) in 9%, 8 to 50 hours after the dose. Asked at the end of the study, 67% of 141 volunteers called the experience positive, 18% neutral and 15% disappointing or bad; 19% would probably not take MDMA again, 47% only in another controlled study and 34% perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known. Why people take MDMA was not studied: none of the five papers asked people who use ecstasy why they do or what they feel in real use; two say, citing other papers, that sociability and empathy are reasons for recreational use. Some people feel little from an amount. Of the reasons usually given, these studies show a start that ranged up to 120 minutes in Zurich; a lowering of Zurich ratings by about 60% by an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion before MDMA; peak blood levels averaging 1.29 times higher in women than in men at the same 125 mg; and, in Chicago and less clearly San Francisco, a lower 'any drug effect' rating with more earlier MDMA use (not for other ratings, and the other way round in Basel); a pill of different content was not tested, as every capsule held a known amount. No one took a second dose within a session, so what happens when people take more was not measured here (controlled second-dose studies are covered in a separate claim). The sessions differ from real life: healthy, screened volunteers (mostly new to MDMA in Basel and Zurich; earlier use in Chicago and San Francisco) took a known capsule and nothing else, at an amount set by the researchers, in a hospital or laboratory room (22.7 degrees Celsius in Basel) with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco; in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis people were alone and gave higher 'anxious' ratings than at the other sites, which the authors suggest, untested, may reflect company. The end-of-study answers came from people given MDMA by researchers, not from people who chose it, and heat, crowds and other drugs were not part of the MDMA sessions.
plain: In hospital studies, healthy volunteers took MDMA on one day and a dummy pill on another, without being told which. In the biggest set (166 people, four in five new to MDMA; 136 had 125 mg), the average highest rating of how strong the effect was came to 73 to 85 out of 100, against 4 after the dummy pill, and of how good it was to 77 to 82 (3 or 4 after the dummy pill). It began about half an hour after the dose and lasted about four hours; 4 of the 166 reported no effect. Volunteers also felt happy, open and close to others, though the findings on closeness are less sure. The same sessions brought unwanted effects. The average highest rating of a bad effect was 13 to 24 out of 100 (2 after the dummy pill). In the first 6 hours, each of these affected 40 to 59 in 100 people: less appetite, a dry mouth, trouble concentrating, cold feet, sweating and a clenched jaw (0 to 6 in 100 after the dummy pill). A day later, 33 in 100 had a headache (15 after the dummy pill) and 30 in 100 low energy (3). Asked at the end of the study, 67 in 100 called the experience positive and 15 in 100 disappointing or bad. Some people feel little from an amount: the studies show a slow start in some people, a much weaker effect after an antidepressant given first, and higher blood levels in women than in men at the same amount. Nobody took more in a session, so that was not tested. The volunteers were healthy, mostly new to MDMA, took a known amount and had researchers with them. No paper asked why people take MDMA.
population: Healthy, screened adults, aged 18 to 45 in the largest set, in research laboratories: 166 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel (83 women, 83 men; mean age 24.5; four in five new to MDMA; 30 people took 75 mg and 136 took 125 mg), 32 in a Basel study probably within them (22 new to MDMA), 16 in Zurich (12 men, 4 women; 13 had never taken MDMA), 9 in Chicago with earlier ecstasy use (7 men, 2 women; 2 to 300 occasions) and, in a three-site pooled analysis that may overlap the others, 220 (Basel 80, Chicago 95, San Francisco 45; lifetime MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions; 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory)
exposure: A single oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride in capsules, given double blind by researchers in a hospital or laboratory (study conditions: 125 mg or 75 mg in Basel; 1.5 mg/kg in Zurich, Chicago and San Francisco; a fixed 125 mg in the Basel part of the three-site analysis; 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order in the Chicago brain-imaging study), with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco, people alone in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis, no other drug, and ratings made at set times; in Zurich, MDMA after an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion was also tested
comparator: Placebo in the same people on another day (double-blind crossover; in Chicago the placebo session was placed at random among ascending doses); sites and earlier-use groups are compared across different people; in Zurich, MDMA after a citalopram infusion in the same people
outcome: Self-ratings of drug effects on 0 to 100 lines (any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, feeling happy, open, close to others, sociable, stimulated, anxious) and mood and altered-state scales; time to onset, peak and end of the effect; physical complaints on a 66-item list up to 6 hours and at 24 hours; end-of-study answers on the overall experience and on taking MDMA again; empathy and money-sharing tests as secondary outcomes
magnitude: Basel pooled analysis (166 people; 125 mg n = 136, 75 mg n = 30), highest self-rating on a 0 to 100 line, mean (SD), MDMA against placebo, at 125 mg: any drug effect women 85 (20) against 4 (8), men 73 (24) against 4 (13); good drug effect women 82 (25) against 3 (10), men 77 (23) against 4 (15); bad drug effect women 24 (24) against 2 (10), men 13 (22) against 2 (10); at 75 mg any drug effect 59 (29) and 56 (32), good 60 (28) and 57 (33), bad 35 (33) and 7 (11). Drug effect F(1,162) 652, 585 and 44 (p < 0.001); women's bad-effect ratings stayed higher after allowing for dose per kilogram (F 20.0) and blood level (F 21.5), both p < 0.001. Four of the 166 reported no effect; onset 33 (SD 24) minutes, peak 1.6 (0.8) hours, duration 4.2 (1.3) hours (range 1.4 to 8.2). Complaints, MDMA against placebo (of 166), up to 6 hours: lack of appetite 59% against 2%, dry mouth 55% against 2%, difficulty concentrating 46% against 6%, cold feet 42% against 4%, sweating 41% against 0, jaw clenching 40% against 1% (134 asked), restless legs 37%, dizziness 34%, hot flushes 31%, heart palpitations 24% (each 0 to 1% on placebo), nausea 11% against 1%, anxiety 9 people (printed as 6%; 9 of 166 is 5.4%, editors' calculation) against 0, headache 25% against 16% (not significant); at 24 hours: lack of appetite 31% against 1%, headache 33% against 15%, lack of energy 30% against 3%. No serious adverse event; depressed mood 4% after 125 mg; flashbacks 12 of 141 (9%) at 8 to 50 hours. End of study (141 asked): experience positive 95 (67%), neutral 25 (18%), disappointing or bad 21 (15%); would probably not take MDMA again 27 (19%), only in another controlled study 66 (47%), perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known 48 (34%). At 125 mg women's peak blood level averaged 1.29 times men's. Basel, 32 people: feeling happy F(1,31) 120.59, open 80.77, close to others 67.52 (p < 0.001); well-being 37.00, extroversion 40.58, activity 24.48; anxiety not raised; empathy test explicit F 6.05 (p = 0.019), implicit 4.29 (p = 0.047), men only on post hoc tests; money sharing F 4.42 (p = 0.044), men p = 0.008. Zurich, 16 people, mean % of the highest possible score (SE): positive mood 40.1 (6.6) against 0.6 on placebo; derealization 32.7 (7.0) against 0.4; thought disorder 24.8 (6.0) against 0.0; onset 20 to 120 (mean 45) minutes; about 60% lower after citalopram (authors' figure). Chicago, 9 people: 'sociable' change at 135 minutes -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg (1.5 mg/kg against placebo p = .04, marginal); friendliness scale F 1.3, not significant. Three sites, 220 people: peak ratings of any drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ by site (p = 0.07 to 1.00; no means printed); earlier use and the any-drug-effect rating: 6.8 points lower per unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7), 13.5 higher in Basel (CI 1.63 to 25.3; fewer than three earlier uses).

evidence.locator: Methods > Study design, 1st paragraph; Methods > Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods > Study drug, 1st paragraph (p. 577, into p. 578)
evidence.extracted: Pooled analysis of nine double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies, all at the University Hospital Basel and all registered (the registrations listed include NCT01386177 and NCT01465685), of 166 psychiatrically screened, healthy European or Caucasian adults aged 18 to 45 (mean 24.5, SD 4; equal numbers of women and men; mean weight 69 kg), mostly recruited on the university campus and paid. 30 people (15 men, 15 women) took a single 75 mg dose and 136 took 125 mg (68 men, 68 women; 24 once, 112 twice, once alone and once with another drug at least seven days apart); this paper analyses the sessions of MDMA alone against placebo. Excluded: psychiatric disorder, physical illness, illicit drug use more than five times in a lifetime (past cannabis excepted) and any in the last two months or during the study (urine tests). 59 had earlier drug experience of 1 to 5 times, 34 of them with MDMA (1 to 4 times). MDMA hydrochloride in gelatin capsules (25 or 100 mg), not adjusted for body weight or sex: 1.7 mg/kg on average (SD 0.4; range 0.8 to 2.7). The authors state that similar amounts are found in ecstasy pills (citing another paper, not read).

evidence.locator: Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph and 3rd paragraph; Methods > Blood sampling and EOS visit, 1st paragraph (p. 578)
evidence.extracted: Self-ratings on 100-mm lines (0 to 100%) from 'not at all' to 'extremely': 'any drug effect', 'good drug effect' and 'bad drug effect', before and at 0, 0.33, 0.67, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5 and 6 hours after the capsule (some time points missing in two studies). Onset, offset and duration were taken from each person's 'any drug effect' curve with 10% of their own peak as the threshold; four people who reported no subjective effect were left out of that analysis. Complaints: a 66-item List of Complaints (bruxism added, used in 134 people), asked 3 to 6 hours (acute) and 24 hours (subacute) after the dose; adverse events from 24 hours to 14 days were also asked about. At the end-of-study visit, on average 29 days (SD 22) after the last of one or two MDMA sessions (with or without a pretreatment drug), volunteers were asked to rate the duration of the response, whether the experience was positive or negative, whether the clinical setting influenced it, whether they would take MDMA again and in what setting, and whether they had 'flashbacks'; these questions were put to 141 volunteers. The paper does not say which session the answers refer to.

evidence.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph; Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph (p. 580)
evidence.extracted: Time course of 'any drug effect' after MDMA alone (four people who reported no effect were left out): onset 33 minutes (SD 24), peak 1.6 hours (SD 0.8), duration 4.2 hours (SD 1.3; range 1.4 to 8.2), with no sex or dose difference in duration; at the end-of-study visit volunteers recalled the duration as 4.0 hours (SD 2.9). MDMA raised 'any drug effect' and 'good drug effect' above placebo, both more at 125 than at 75 mg; a drug-by-sex interaction that was nearly significant: women tended to give higher 'any drug effect' ratings. MDMA also raised 'bad drug effect' ratings, not dose-dependent and higher in women than in men, still with dose per kilogram as a covariate (F(1,162) 20.0, p < 0.001) and with peak blood level as a covariate (F 21.5, p < 0.001). The mean room temperature was 22.7 degrees Celsius (SD 0.6).

evidence.locator: Table 1, rows 'Any drug effect', 'Good drug effect' and 'Bad drug effect' (all columns)
evidence.extracted: Highest self-rating after the dose, mean (SD), MDMA against placebo; 125 mg (68 women, 68 men) then 75 mg (15 and 15). Any drug effect: women 85 (20) against 4 (8) and 59 (29) against 3 (6); men 73 (24) against 4 (13) and 56 (32) against 6 (9). Good drug effect: women 82 (25) against 3 (10) and 60 (28) against 6 (13); men 77 (23) against 4 (15) and 57 (33) against 7 (12). Bad drug effect: women 24 (24) against 2 (10) and 35 (33) against 4 (13); men 13 (22) against 2 (10) and 7 (11) against 6 (16). Drug effect F(1,162): any 652, good 585, bad 44 (p < 0.001); drug-by-dose: any 20 (p < 0.001), good 20 (printed p < 0.01), bad 0.001 (not significant); drug-by-sex: any 3.4 (p = 0.068), good 0.9 (not significant), bad 16 (p < 0.001); drug-by-dose-by-sex for bad 3.6 (p = 0.059).

evidence.locator: Results > Adverse effects of MDMA, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 580, 2nd paragraph continued on p. 582); Table 2, rows 'List of complaints score' (p. 582); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 584)
evidence.extracted: Rise in the total List of Complaints score, MDMA against placebo, mean (SD): acute (up to 6 hours) 8.8 (5.9) in women and 6.4 (6.8) in men, subacute (24 hours) 5.4 (5.5) and 3.0 (5.0); the sex difference held after allowing for dose per kilogram or blood level (p < 0.05). Table 2, MDMA against placebo: 125 mg acute 10.0 (6.6) against 1.7 (2.3), subacute 5.7 (5.6) against 0.9 (2.2); 75 mg acute 5.6 (4.5) against 1.6 (2.1), subacute 2.9 (4.1) against 0.9 (1.5). Acute anxiety was reported by nine people (6%) after 125 mg and none after 75 mg. No serious adverse events were reported. From 24 hours to 7 to 14 days: headache 6% after 125 mg, 7% after 75 mg and 5% after placebo; depressed mood 4% after 125 mg (0% otherwise); none reported significantly more often after MDMA than after placebo. In the 125 mg studies 12 people (9%) reported 'flashbacks' 1 to 3 times (one eight times), on average 26 hours (SD 15; range 8 to 50) after the dose, with no sex difference; the Discussion says all 12 were within 8 to 50 hours and that no persisting perceptual change was found in this controlled setting.

evidence.locator: Table 3, all rows; columns 'Placebo' and 'MDMA', 'Up to 6 h' and '24 h'
evidence.extracted: Complaints, MDMA against placebo, n (%) of 166: up to 6 hours lack of appetite 98 (59%) against 3 (2%); dry mouth 91 (55%) against 3 (2%); difficulty concentrating 76 (46%) against 10 (6%); cold feet 69 (42%) against 7 (4%); sweating 68 (41%) against 0; jaw clenching 54 (40%, of 134 asked) against 1 (1%); restless legs 62 (37%) against 2 (1%); dizziness 57 (34%) against 2 (1%); hot flushes 52 (31%) against 0; heart palpitations 40 (24%) against 2 (1%); lack of energy 38 (23%) against 23 (14%); nausea 19 (11%) against 2 (1%); anxiety 9 (6%) against 0; headache 42 (25%) against 27 (16%), not significantly different. At 24 hours: lack of appetite 52 (31%) against 1 (1%); dry mouth 37 (23%) against 3 (2%); difficulty concentrating 35 (22%) against 4 (2%); headache 55 (33%) against 25 (15%); lack of energy 49 (30%) against 5 (3%); jaw clenching 19 (14%) against 1 (1%); hot flushes 12 (7%) against 0; restless legs 12 (7%) against 2 (1%); dizziness 12 (7%) against 3 (2%); heart palpitations 11 (7%) against 1 (1%); cold feet 10 (6%) against 2 (1%); nausea 9 (6%) against 1 (1%); sweating 7 (4%) against 0; anxiety 3 (2%) against 0, not significant. Both doses are pooled (total n = 166).

evidence.locator: Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph (p. 582, right column, continued on pp. 583 and 584)
evidence.extracted: Asked at the end of the study: 80% were new to MDMA, the rest had at most four earlier exposures. Of 141 volunteers asked whether they would consider taking MDMA again, 27 (19%) probably not under any circumstances; 66 (47%) not recreationally but possibly in another study under controlled conditions; 48 (34%) possibly in a recreational setting but only if identity, purity and dose were known, 24 of these 48 (50%) having taken illicit drugs before, including MDMA; only 13 considered a club setting. Overall experience: 95 (67%) positive, 25 (18%) neutral, 21 (15%) disappointing or bad, with no sex differences. The controlled setting had no impact for 51 (36%) and was important for the type of experience, reassuring and made them feel safe for 90 (64%); women rated the setting as more important than men (F(1,139) 12.4, p < 0.001).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 584, left column)
evidence.extracted: The authors read their data as clearly greater positive than negative acute subjective effects and a state of predominantly positive mood across laboratories (citing other papers, not read), with one exception; modest apprehension anxiety in some volunteers, reported as an acute adverse effect by 7% after 125 mg and not after 75 mg (the Results say nine people, 6%); anxiety could be reduced by verbal support in all of the volunteers and no benzodiazepine was used; no cases of severe anxiety or panic attacks; psychological distress minimal (no distress measure is reported apart from the 'bad drug effect' rating and the one-item anxiety complaint); overall positive experiences retrospectively in two-thirds and 15% disappointed or with bad experiences. They contrast this with panic attacks and agitation or aggression described in people who use ecstasy and present to emergency departments (cited from other papers, not read).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 584, right column); Discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs (p. 585)
evidence.extracted: The authors suggest that no controlled study has reported a body temperature above 40 degrees possibly because volunteers had moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded environment, unlike some recreational settings. In their research setting a research assistant is always present, similar to a therapy session and unlike some other experimental settings; participants typically had no or very little earlier MDMA experience; the response may differ in people with psychiatric disorders compared with volunteers screened to be psychiatrically healthy; limits: only psychiatrically healthy and mostly young volunteers; hyponatraemia, neurocognitive function and long-term problems not assessed; 278 sessions too few to exclude events at 0.1 to 1%.

evidence.locator: Methods > Study drug, 1st paragraph (p. 578); Table 1, rows 'Cmax' (p. 581); Results > Plasma concentrations of MDMA, 1st paragraph (p. 582); Discussion, 8th paragraph (p. 585)
evidence.extracted: Dose per kilogram at 125 mg: 1.7 (SD 0.2) in men and 2.1 (SD 0.3) in women. Peak blood MDMA level (Cmax) at 125 mg: women 252 (SD 40) and men 195 (SD 37) ng/mL; at the same 125 mg women had on average 1.29 times the Cmax and 1.26 times the 6-hour exposure of men. The authors say the 1.29 could be explained mainly by women's 1.24-fold lower body weight, and that subjective 'bad drug effect' ratings and other adverse effects were greater in women than in men, also after correcting for dose per kilogram or blood level.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; Methods and Materials > Procedure, Dependent Measures, and Drug, 1st paragraph; Results > Participants, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Three laboratories pooled, 220 volunteers (44% women; age 25.4, SD 5.2; weight 68.8 kg): San Francisco 45 (20 women, 25 men; 1.5 mg/kg; researchers present; 11 am), Chicago 95 (37 women, 58 men; 1.5 mg/kg; people alone; 9:30 am; told they might receive a stimulant, sedative, cannabinoid or placebo) and Basel 80 (40 women, 40 men; a fixed 125 mg, 1.89 mg/kg (SD 0.33); researchers present; 8 to 9 am; told MDMA or placebo); oral capsules, double blind. Lifetime MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions: San Francisco 32.8 (SD 37.0), Chicago 13.1 (13.5), Basel 0.6 (0.6); 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory. The authors say some of the data were published earlier (Harris 2002, Bedi 2010, Hysek 2012) and some not (San Francisco, Chicago).

evidence.locator: Results > Acute Effects of MDMA across Sites, 1st paragraph; Figures 1 and 2
evidence.extracted: MDMA raised heart rate and blood pressure to a similar degree at the three sites (site comparisons p = 0.15 to 1.00) and gave similar reports on most subjective ratings; peak ratings of 'any drug effect', 'drug liking' and 'stimulated' after MDMA did not differ between sites (p = 0.07 to 1.00). Minor differences: after MDMA Chicago volunteers gave higher peak 'anxious' ratings than San Francisco and Basel volunteers, and San Francisco volunteers higher 'closeness to others' than Basel volunteers (p < 0.05 for each); after placebo Chicago volunteers gave higher peak 'any drug effect' and 'drug liking' than the other two sites (p < 0.01). The values are in figures that were not extracted; the text prints no means or effect sizes, and no significant difference is not proof of equality.

evidence.locator: Results > Relationship between acute drug-related effects and MDMA use history, 1st paragraph; Figure 3
evidence.extracted: The 'any drug effect' rating after MDMA related to lifetime MDMA use differently by site (use-by-site F(2, 218) = 4.74, p = 0.010). It fell by 6.8 points (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7) per unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago, by 5.8 (CI -1.00 to 12.53; p = 0.094) in San Francisco and by 6.1 (CI 2.18 to 10.0) in the two together; in Basel, where people had used MDMA fewer than three times or not at all, it rose by 13.5 (CI 1.63 to 25.3). No other relation between earlier use and an acute effect reached significance. The log base is not stated, so the slopes cannot be converted to points per additional use.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st, 3rd, 5th and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors describe the use-history finding as modest evidence of tolerance in people with heavier use (1st paragraph). They suggest, without testing it, that having researchers in the room (San Francisco, Basel) may have raised prosocial ratings and lowered negative ratings compared with being alone (Chicago), and note that closeness ratings fell with earlier use in San Francisco at trend level (p = 0.07) (3rd paragraph). They call the data the strongest support so far for repeated use weakening the subjective experience, and little support for a much stronger first experience; in Basel, responses reflected only the first to third experience, and people may come to identify the drug effect more accurately across those first experiences (5th paragraph). Other explanations they offer: people with heavier use may also use other potent drugs, tolerance may be specific to the setting, and the 'any drug effect' item is a global rating that may be more sensitive than the others (6th paragraph).

evidence.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors state, citing earlier papers that were not read, that there is some evidence that chronic tolerance develops to the 'positive' subjective effects of MDMA, and that apparent decreases in effect may instead result from changes in the purity of MDMA tablets over time or place. No new data.

evidence.locator: Materials and Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph; Experimental protocol, 1st paragraph; Study drug, 1st paragraph; Measures > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: 32 healthy volunteers (16 men, 16 women), mean age 25 (SD 3; range 20 to 31), from the University of Basel campus; excluded: psychiatric or physical illness, smoking, illicit drug use more than five times in a lifetime (past cannabis excepted) and any in the last 2 months (urine tests); 22 completely new to MDMA and 10 with fewer than five earlier uses; 19 had used cannabis more than five times and 15 other illicit drugs one to four times; women were tested in the follicular phase. Double-blind, placebo-controlled, random-order crossover; MDMA 125 mg (mean 1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.30) and identical placebo capsules, at least 10 days apart; registered (NCT01386177 and NCT01465685); paid. Visual analogue scales for 'happy', 'open' and 'close to others', and the 60-item Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AMRS); repeated measures were expressed as the peak change from baseline.

evidence.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
evidence.extracted: MDMA raised visual analogue ratings of feeling happy (F(1,31) = 120.59), open (80.77) and close to others (67.52), all P < 0.001, and AMRS scores for activity (24.48), inactivity (7.72, P = 0.009), extroversion (40.58), introversion (10.05, P = 0.003), well-being (37.00), emotional excitation (28.46) and dreaminess (25.48), the rest P < 0.001, but not for anxiety. A sex-by-treatment interaction for 'happy' (F(1,31) = 10.49, P = 0.003), but no difference between men and women after MDMA on post hoc tests; no other sex-by-treatment interaction. The text prints no means; they are in Figure 1 and in Supplementary Table S1 (not read).

evidence.locator: Results > Empathy, 1st paragraph; Results > Social Value Orientation, 1st paragraph; Results > Facial emotion recognition, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Empathy test: MDMA raised explicit and implicit emotional empathy ratings across all volunteers (F(1,31) = 6.05, P = 0.019; 4.29, P = 0.047), significantly for positive scenes (8.60, P = 0.006; 5.02, P = 0.032) and not for negative scenes; interaction with sex for implicit empathy (4.68, P = 0.039) and a trend for explicit (3.03, P = 0.092); post hoc, the rises were significant in men only (P = 0.025 explicit, 0.022 implicit); cognitive empathy unchanged. Money allocation (Social Value Orientation): the prosocial angle rose (F(1,31) = 4.42, P = 0.044) with a sex interaction (5.52, P = 0.026); post hoc significant in men (P = 0.008) and not in women; the inequality-aversion index tended to fall (F(1,20) = 3.39, P = 0.079). Face recognition: accuracy fell overall (F(1,31) = 28.63, P < 0.001), for fearful (14.90), angry (18.60), disgusted (5.81, P = 0.022) and surprised (9.79, P = 0.004) faces but not happy faces (0.27, P = 0.607); the fall was significant in women and not in men.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: one dose only, relatively high with obvious subjective effects; although the design was double blind with identical placebo, most volunteers realised which treatment they had been given, so unblinding may have biased task performance; the evaluation of many aspects of social cognition required a relatively large number of statistical comparisons. They say the dose was chosen to correspond to those typically used in recreational settings (citing another paper, not read) or in clinical trials; lower doses and an active placebo could be used in future studies.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors state, citing earlier laboratory and clinical papers rather than surveys of people who use ecstasy (not read), that MDMA produces subjective prosocial feelings and that enhancing empathy and sociability is also considered a major reason for the recreational use of MDMA and for its therapeutic effects in psychotherapy. This paper presents no data on why people take MDMA.

evidence.locator: Materials and Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph; Protocol, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 9 healthy, right-handed volunteers (7 men, 2 women; mean age 24.0, SD 3.2; range 18 to 29), recruited by on-line advertisements and word of mouth, with earlier ecstasy use of 2 to 300 occasions (mean 63.9, SD 94.9; 4 of 9 in the past year; last use 0.5 to 24 months earlier); all had used cannabis, 8 stimulants and 7 hallucinogens; in the past month 5 smoked cigarettes daily. Three-session double-blind design within people: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order and placebo placed at random, at least 6 days apart; sessions began at noon; lactose capsules; abstinence from cannabis for 7 days, alcohol for 24 hours and other drugs for 48 hours, checked by urine, saliva and breath tests; after the capsule volunteers stayed in hospital at least 4.5 hours, in a comfortable laboratory environment.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Peak 'feel drug' rating (Drug Effects Questionnaire; change from before the capsule) 14.5 on placebo, 57.1 at 0.75 mg/kg and 91.8 at 1.5 mg/kg (F(2,16) 98.6; each dose above placebo and 1.5 above 0.75 mg/kg on post hoc tests, threshold p < .01); peak systolic pressure rose 4.8, 34.8 and 48.1 mm Hg and heart rate -5.3, 19.7 and 35.3 beats a minute; no serious adverse effects. 'Sociable' (visual analogue scale), change from baseline at 135 minutes: -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 mg/kg and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg (drug-by-time F(8,64) 3.1, partial eta-squared .28; at 135 minutes F(2,16) 7.3); 1.5 against 0.75 mg/kg t(8) 3.8 (p < .01); 1.5 mg/kg against placebo t(8) 2.5 (p = .04, called marginal against the paper's p < .01 threshold for post hoc tests); 0.75 mg/kg against placebo not different (t(8) 0.5). The Profile of Mood States Friendliness scale showed a similar pattern that was not significant (F(2,16) 1.3). Accuracy and speed of recognising emotional faces did not change.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors write that increased sociability and decreased defensiveness are cited by people who use ecstasy as a motivator to use it (citing Sumnall 2006, not read here) and that people who use ecstasy recreationally describe feeling sociable after it (Discussion, citing the same paper); they also cite controlled human studies of raised sociability ratings, and say that advocates of psychotherapeutic use argue MDMA increases openness to the therapeutic process (citing Parrott 2007, not read here). This paper's own data do not address why people take MDMA.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 8th to 11th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The drug increased subjective sociability only at the higher dose (1.5 mg/kg), while at the lower dose (0.75 mg/kg) it raised the ventral striatum response to happy faces without changing sociability ratings. The authors call the findings preliminary: the sample was small (9) and replication in a larger sample is needed; only two brain regions were chosen in advance; MDMA may have blood-flow effects on the signal; all volunteers had earlier ecstasy exposure, varying widely (they found no correlation between use variables and the brain signal); doses were given in ascending order for safety, which may have influenced outcomes, with at least 6 days between sessions (average 10.72, SD 7.15) and no effect of session order found; no plasma MDMA was measured.

evidence.locator: Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Substances and Dosing, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Study Design, 1st paragraph (p. 514, continued on p. 515); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 515)
evidence.extracted: 16 healthy volunteers (12 men, 4 women; aged 21 to 39, mean 27.4, SD 4.4) recruited at the University Hospital and the Medical School of Zurich, high-school educated, all but one university students or physicians; six had earlier recreational drug experience, three of them with ecstasy, so 13 had never tried it. Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person design with four counterbalanced conditions at least 14 days apart (placebo-placebo, citalopram-placebo, placebo-MDMA, citalopram-MDMA); citalopram 40 mg (or saline) by infusion over 90 minutes, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg, SD 10) or placebo capsules by mouth; psychometric ratings once, 120 minutes after MDMA. MDMA alone mainly produced a state of positive mood, moderate derealization, heightened sensory awareness and a slight rise in psychomotor drive; the subjective effect began 20 to 120 minutes after intake (mean 45), peaked 15 to 30 minutes later and lasted a mean of 3 hours. After citalopram the effect was markedly reduced but lasted a mean of 5 hours. Side effects and cardiovascular changes from the same sessions are to be reported separately.

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 516)
evidence.extracted: Adjective Mood Rating Scale after MDMA against placebo: raised 'heightened mood' (p < .03), 'self-confidence' (p < .02), 'extroversion' (p < .01), 'introversion' (p < .05), 'emotional excitability' (p < .01), 'sensitivity' (p < .03) and 'thoughtfulness-contemplativeness' (p < .002); 'tiredness' lowered (p < .05) and 'dazed state' raised (p < .02); no change in 'aggression-anger', 'apprehension-anxiety' or 'depressiveness'; 'efficiency-activation' not raised, although a moderate rise in psychomotor drive was shown. The authors' summary: a state of enhanced mood with happiness, euphoria and in some volunteers mania-like experience, increased self-confidence and extroversion; moderate derealization, depersonalization and thought disorder (accelerated thinking, thought blocking and impaired decision making) without anxiety or panic reactions; no evidence of delusional thinking; no hallucinations but an intensification of visual, tactile and acoustic perception and changes in the meaning of the surroundings; only a slight rise in psychomotor drive.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (all rows and columns)
evidence.extracted: Altered States of Consciousness scale item clusters, mean percent of the highest possible score (SE), n = 16, placebo then MDMA then citalopram-MDMA: positive basic mood 0.6, 40.1 (6.6), 16.4; derealization 0.4, 32.7 (7.0), 12.6; depersonalization 0.0, 24.5 (6.7), 10.5; alterations of the sense of time 0.8, 30.9 (7.6), 13.1; mania-like experience 0.3, 26.6 (6.2), 6.7; frightening derealization 0.0, 8.5 (3.7), 2.1; thought disorder 0.0, 24.8 (6.0), 8.6; delusion 0.0, 10.4 (5.6), 1.5; loss of thought control 0.0, 14.1 (5.6), 2.8; loss of body control 0.2, 11.9 (3.6), 5.3; hallucinations 0.1, 9.7 (3.1), 3.6; synesthesia 0.0, 12.8 (4.6), 8.0; changed meaning of percepts 0.6, 37.3 (7.2), 14.1; facilitated recollection 0.0, 18.4 (6.2), 7.6; facilitated imagination 0.7, 27.2 (8.7), 6.6. MDMA raised most clusters above placebo (p < .05) but not delusion or hallucinations; citalopram pretreatment lowered most of the MDMA-induced scores (p < .05).

evidence.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (p. 518, continued on p. 519); concluding paragraph (p. 519, right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors say citalopram attenuated the effects of MDMA by about 60 percent, not fully, which they do not put down to too little citalopram: all volunteers received 40 mg whatever their weight, with no correlation between dose per kilogram and the size of the lowering, and in a pilot study two people given 60 or 80 mg had the effects of MDMA blocked to a degree comparable to 40 mg. They also say citalopram prolonged the effects by up to two hours compared with MDMA alone and offer two possible reasons (a metabolic interaction, or competition at the uptake site).

risk_of_bias.note: The comparison that carries the claim, MDMA against placebo in the same people, is at worst some concerns on the cards (session order is not described in the Basel pooled paper, the three-site paper or the Chicago paper), but the ratings are self-reports by volunteers who could tell what they had been given: the effects are obvious, the Basel authors say most volunteers realised which treatment they had, and no paper tested the blind. The Basel papers also tested about 40 to 60 outcomes without correction. The size of the differences (about 80 against about 4 out of 100 for a good effect at 125 mg in 136 people) limits how much expectation can explain, so one level, not two. The social, empathy, sex-specific and earlier-use findings are worded as weaker and are not rated separately.

inconsistency.note: The direction agrees at Basel, Zurich, Chicago and San Francisco for ratings of drug effect, liking and good effect. Where results differ (closeness higher in San Francisco than in Basel, 'anxious' higher in Chicago, sociability marginal and only at the higher dose, earlier use opposite in Basel), the statement says so and does not rest on them.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the statement describes volunteers in laboratory sessions and says where they differ from real life (healthy, screened, mostly new to MDMA, a fixed known amount, a hospital room with researchers present). It does not say what MDMA feels like in real use or why people take it, which none of these papers measured.

imprecision.note: 166 people for the main ratings, with differences far larger than their spread (SDs of 20 to 33 around averages of 56 to 85, against 3 to 7 on placebo). The smaller samples (16, 9, 32) carry the secondary findings and are described as such; no intervals are printed for the ratings.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: the Basel and three-site papers are pooled analyses by the teams that ran the studies, the three-site pool is not registered, and the registry records of the Basel studies were not read. No sign of selective omission, but unpublished studies cannot be excluded.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled double-blind within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Moderate for the statement that, in healthy volunteers in laboratory sessions, a single dose of MDMA raised self-rated drug effect and good effect above placebo (about 80 against about 4 out of 100 at 125 mg, in 136 people), began within about an hour, lasted about four hours, and was accompanied by bad-effect ratings and physical complaints in the same sessions. The parts that rest on one small study or on marginal or post hoc tests (sociability in 9 people, the empathy and money-sharing tests, face recognition, the earlier-use relation, the effect of citalopram) are worded as such and would be rated lower on their own; a separate claim could carry them. The certainty does not extend to real use or to why people take MDMA, which these studies did not measure. Status replicated: the direction agrees at four places, but the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers share a senior author and one author (Liechti) is on four of the five papers (the Basel pooled paper, the Basel empathy paper, the Zurich paper and the three-site paper, which also includes the Chicago senior author), so the four places are not fully independent. The claim gives no advice on amounts or timing, and describing the effects people rated as good is a finding, not encouragement.

verification.flag_note: Sumnall et al. (2006) and Boys et al. (2001), the two papers meant to say why people take MDMA from their own accounts, were not read (their PDFs had not been saved when this was drafted), so 'why people take MDMA' rests on two papers' second-hand statements only and the claim says that none of the papers read asked; redraft when both are read. The Basel overlap is probable but not stated: both registrations of the 32-person study are on the pooled paper's list of nine, and the three-site paper's Basel 80 may sit inside the 166. The Chicago 9-person study and the Chicago part of the three-site paper share a senior author, and the three-site paper says some of its data were published earlier (overlap with the 9 not stated). Liechti is an author of four of the five papers (Basel pooled, Basel empathy, Zurich and the three-site paper). The three-site paper prints no means (figures not read) and its use-history slopes have no stated log base; the 32-person paper's supplementary table was not read; the 9-person paper's abstract states the sociability result against placebo more strongly than its own post hoc threshold (p = .04 against .01). The sociability, empathy and earlier-use findings are single-study and could be split into their own claim. The sc_liechti_2000 card was written by AI reader 51; these anchors were located from the PDF by this reader. The Basel pooled card was extended (additive; staged in _incoming/mdma/) with the ratings, complaints and end-of-study findings.
